blog_publication/Nov9_2025.content:
放学后趴在走廊的栏杆上，透过几乎是光秃秃的梧桐树枝向西望去。太阳已经不见了，只剩微微泛红的天边和不远处工地的剪影。我忽然意识到已经立冬了。
11月的风恶毒地钻进我的领子。我只能将双手死死抱在胸前，眯着眼睛往后门走去。那时候nsfz的后门还人来人往，没有因为疫情封闭，也没有店因此关门停业。如果是夏天，我会在风中闻到蛋包饭的香味，或许还有炸鸡和可乐。但是现在鼻腔里只有一股金属的血腥味。又一年后的冬天，后门再也没对我们敞开过，对其印象也停留在了一个天黑的很早的冬日，模糊的视线，昏暗的小巷，而没有一丝嗅觉上的记忆了。
我一直对饺子无感，可我竟然在主动找能吃饺子的地方。这甚至是我第一次听说立冬有这个习俗。吃什么都无所谓，只是觉得该好好庆祝一下冬天。即使冬天把我冻的瑟瑟发抖我也喜欢冬天，喜欢把自己挪回室内时身体重新焕发生机的感觉，喜欢大脑晕乎乎的幸福的感觉。我刻意避开了平时会去的那家馄炖店，因为我知道走上二楼一定会看到那群男的在玩原神，多少会有点扫兴。于是我多往前走了两步，去了一家很少去的面馆。我张望了一下，大家在面馆里都点的是饺子。
五年后，在一个离南京十万八千里的城市，在宾大金黄色的秋天里上几人在没头没脑的说寒假要做的事。dzp说，冬天不就应该除了谈恋爱什么事情都不干吗。
好久没有从任何一个朋友嘴巴里听到过这么正确的话了。我由衷的认为她是天才。她说这话的时候正牵着男朋友在草坪上走，落叶在脚下发出嘎吱嘎吱的声响。nsfz那条鹅卵石小路一到十月也会铺满褐色的梧桐叶，像秋天自身一般脆弱易碎。九点半晚自习课间的喧闹声逐渐归于平静，谁在那里踩一脚梧桐叶，六楼的窗边能听的一清二楚。如果传来的是急促的刺啦刺啦声，可能是老师正在往班上赶；但如果每一声都拖的长长的，仿佛能让你感受到叶子碎裂的纹路，那一定是还在私会的欲说还休的情侣。
而此时此刻这样面馆里坐满了这样的情侣，狭小的店面里只有我突兀的站在那。我鼓起勇气想去问一对情侣能不能拼个桌，还没开口椅子就被老板一把薅起来，递给门口另外一对情侣。
几年后我和王子枫专程去看了眼后门，聊起这家面馆，他也说老板的态度很差，总是忽视一个人来的顾客。我说到那个立冬的晚上，说到我经常幻想在放学的傍晚有人能和我并肩走着，从炸鸡店游荡到回龙桥的花店，从未名湖走到标本林，看路灯把我们的影子拉得很长很长。
王子枫说唉冬天。他说不出来冬天应该谈恋爱以外什么事都不干这种话不是因为他不是天才，只是他已经很久没有和人一起走过铺满梧桐叶的鹅卵石小路了。

blog_publication/Oct26_2025.title: Oct26_2025
blog_publication/Oct26_2025.content:
我在maudlin讲fact, fiction, and forecast的时候走了神，因为我课前根本没看这本书。他的小狗正屁股对着我，我开始思考它什么时候屁颠屁颠跑过来趴我腿上。它毛茸茸的，很像今天的云朵。上学路上我幽怨的盯着天空，想为什么好天气永远在上学的时候出现。
恍惚间听到老师说在他想来世界有种最坏的可能，可能一切只存在了一秒，在此之前所有记忆全是幻觉。
听上去是个很老掉牙的skepticism问题，毕竟这本书就是个重生版的hume。我不知道怎么反驳他。我想这确实有可能，毕竟一秒钟前我在白日做梦，或许世界诞生于梦醒时分，梦到的东西只是世界解的initial condition。我很讨厌康德用一些超自然和自己不承认是心理学的心理学去反驳他的做法。
maudlin说拒绝这种可能也不实用。哪怕世界在此刻才开始运转，也不会影响任何我们对世界的认知，物理学的定律不会因此发生变化，历史书也不会改写。我们只是不知道怎么证明这一切确实存在。
而此时此刻maudlin的小狗真钻到了我身边。真是遗憾，抚摸它脑袋时这种触手可及的真实感也没法被证明。承认这一切的真实性似乎不可避免的要多一些ontology上的负担。
我想如果这一切都是真实的话，今天我像往常所有的周二一样九点半被闹钟吵醒，睁开右眼按掉闹钟，继续昏迷到十点半。我在街角的deli慢悠悠的吃完三明治后准备连着第四周迟到，因为这样电梯门在三楼一打开就能看到maudlin的小狗在门口迎接我。我会在门口反复摩挲两遍它毛茸茸的脑袋再进教室。可惜今天失策了，他到的比我还晚。
其实今天我也不是十点半起的床，可能早了十分钟。醒来时太阳在云层中不时探头，光线透过百叶窗让房间不停明暗交替。我想起刚才做的梦，我在没有尽头的荒原里飞奔，穿过白昼，穿过黑夜，穿过光明，穿过阴霾。我知道这不可能是真的，但是经验也无法证明我的inference。
我想起王二想变成天上忽明忽暗的云，但我没有这种想法。这种话只有诗人才说得出来，我不是诗人。我只会想一些不切实际的问题。

phil_public/2_deflationary_accounts_of_t.title: 2_deflationary_accounts_of_truth_handout_horwich
phil_public/2_deflationary_accounts_of_t.content:
truth metaphysics horwich
In summary, Horwich holds that a true proposition should follow the equivalence schema below:
\ulcorner p \urcorner \text{ is true} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad p
There might be some part I forgot about the quotation mark \ulcorner\urcorner.
Highlighted parts, section 5, and the last section were written by me, while the rest was organizing Horwich’s handout.
INTRODUCTION
This document is divided into 5 sections.
In section 1, I’ll indicate how deflationary accounts of truth differ from traditional proposals about the nature of truth — and why a deflationary account is preferable.
In section 2, I’ll begin my assessment of which is the better deflationary account of the meaning of “true” — as between, on the one hand,
(i) My use-theoretic, so-called minimalist suggestion, whose heart is the view that the meaning of the English word “true”, when applied to (or denied of) a proposition, consists in the inclination of English speakers to accept instances of the schema: “The proposition that p is true ↔ p” — which is known as the Equivalence Schema.
And on the other hand,
(ii) Wolfgang Künne’s ingenious, but controversial, definition of “x is true” as
(\exists p)((x = p)\wedge p)
which departs from classical logic by invoking quantification into sentence positions.
It’s worth noting that my above qualification of “the meaning of the English word ‘true’,” by the addition of “when applied to (or denied of) propositions” is essential: because the English word “true” is ambiguous — sometimes used with a meaning that’s very far from the one that my minimalism and Künne’s definition are aiming to capture.
For example, one might say, “She’s a true friend” and “He was a true hero”, where what’s meant (roughly speaking) is “She’s a paradigmatic, or perfect example of a friend” and “He was a paradigmatic, or perfect example of a hero”. But when we describe a certain proposition as true, we are never saying that it’s a perfect, or paradigmatic example of a proposition!!
In section 3, I’ll respond to a valuably challenging essay by the late Sten Lindström, in which he maintains that my Minimalism is substantially inadequate, because of the many truth-claims that it cannot accommodate (or so he argues — but I disagree!)
After that — in the relatively short 4th section of the paper — I turn to the question of whether either of the proposals we have been considering — mine or Künne’s — can accommodate the plausible view that a statement that’s untranslatable into our language might nonetheless be true.
In Section 5 I describe and address a paradox that arises from applying the above-mentioned Equivalence Schema — “The proposition that p is true ↔ p”, to a person’s assertion that what s/he is asserting is not true.
And finally — in light of those discussions — I’ll offer (in section 6) my answers to some provocative questions posed in the announcement of the University of Vienna’s last-September conference on TRUTH:

Is truth definable?
Is propositional quantification coherent?
Do natural languages involve propositional quantification, and in what sense?
What do the answers to these questions mean for philosophical attempts to define or explain truth?


SECTION 1
Each of the proposed traditional accounts of truth took the form of a definition that purported to articulate (i) the meaning of the English word “true” (when it’s predicated of propositions), and (ii) the underlying nature of the property of being true.
Here are some prominent examples of such proposed definitions — each one followed by the grounds for rejecting it:

1. “x is true ↔ x corresponds to a fact”
But: the concept of “correspondence” is itself mysterious, yet unexplained.
And — even worse — it’s arguable that the term of itself — the word “fact”, should be defined as “true proposition”! — In which case 1. defines “true” in terms of itself — which is absurd!!
Tim Maudlin tells me that deflationism is just another kind of correspondence theory. We can revisit this argument later.
To see more about correspondence theory, go check [plato.stanford.edu/entries/truth/#CorRev]. 

The correspondence theory of truth expresses the very natural idea that truth is a content-to-world or word-to-world relation: what we say or think is true or false in virtue of the way the world turns out to be.

Correspondence theory is a very natural way of thinking of the truth as a content-to-world relation.

2. “x is true ↔ the possibility articulated by x is actualized”
But surely, a possibility is simply a proposition (one that could be true).
And calling a proposition “actualized” is just an awkward way of saying that it’s true!!

3. Putnam “x is true ↔ a rational investigation would dictate believing x.”

 There Putnam glosses truth as what would be justified under ideal epistemic conditions. With the pragmatists, Putnam sees the ideal conditions as something which can be approximated, echoing the idea of truth as the end of inquiry. (SEP)

But many truths are inaccessible to our investigations — either too remote, or too deep, or too complex, or too conceptually-alien.
And rational considerations often point away from the truth!
Moreover: rational considerations rarely deliver certainty. And being 90% confident in the truth of 100 independent hypotheses implies that their conjunction is probably false!

4. “x is true ↔ x is almost universally believed”
But: surely everyone could agree on a given point, yet all be mistaken.
Consensus can change over time.
And when people are divided, one of them must be right — but the true one is not almost universally believed.

5. Peirce “x is true ↔ x will be believed in the limit of enquiry.”
But: disagreements may never be ironed out.
Agreement in the very distant future cannot ground truth-claims now.
And even permanent agreement cannot guarantee correctness.

6. William James “x is true ↔ decisions based on assuming x will promote practical success.”
But: actions based on a person’s true beliefs can (unluckily) have catastrophic consequences.
Conversely, false beliefs can (luckily) have life-saving consequences.
James’ idea captures something about the value of true beliefs, but cannot define truth.

5. Foucault “x is true ↔ x is what the political powers pressure us to believe.”
But: political powers often pressure us to believe what is false.
And many matters are ones the regime does not care about.
Power may determine what is taken to be true, but not what is true.

SECTION 2 Künne’s schema
Regarding the two deflationary accounts of truth — mine and Künne’s — I’m confident that almost everyone here is prepared to bet that I will proceed by standing up for my own view, and by criticizing Professor Künne’s view.
But those people would lose their money!!
For I don’t share the common complaint about Künne’s account:

that quantification into sentence positions is unintelligible.
or the implied view that classical logic, with quantifiers

“(\forall x)(Fx)” for “everything is F”
“(\exists x)(Fx)” for “something is F”
there are no sentences of ordinary language, whose logical forms are best captured by quantifying into sentence positions.



On the contrary, quantifying into declarative sentence positions is easy to understand and quite useful.
The term “declarative” is inserted here to make it clear that Künne does not endorse quantification into the position of sentences that are questions like “is the window open?” or imperatives like “open the window!” but only into the positions of sentences that express propositions like “the window is open.”
It is easy to understand quantification in positions of declarative sentences. Consider the excluded middle rule (\forall p) (p\vee \sim p), and to be disposed to accept the schema is to be disposed to accept any instance of the schema p\vee \sim p.
Similarly, for the case of truth, we shall recognize that a person’s disposition to accept instances of the equivalence schema \ulcorner p \urcorner \text{ is true}\Leftrightarrow p amounts to his/her being disposed to accept (\forall p) (\ulcorner p \urcorner \text{ is true}\Leftrightarrow p)
As for Künne’s proposed definition of “true:
(\forall x)\bigg(x\text{ is true}\Leftrightarrow (\exists p)(x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p)\bigg)
I have just offered a defense of Künne’s quantifying with a universal quantifier, into sentence positions. But one might worry that this could not help us to understand his definition of truth, since that definition involves existential quantification into a sentence position.
It could be easily dispelled by propositional logic, and we can turn the statement
(\exists p)(x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p) into
\sim(\forall p)\bigg(\sim (x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p)\bigg)
So the disposition to accept Künne’s equivalence schema consists in the pair of dispositions.
Given acceptance of ”x is true” and "x = \ulcorner p \urcorner" to accept p. And given acceptance of some instance of the schema "x = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p" to accept ”x is true”.
==Comments==： I do not understand what he is talking about in the matter of logic. If we restricted the language to formal language like PA, it could be totally understandable, since we could stipulate the axioms as true propositions. However, here I think every reader would either think the equivalence schema is trivially right or that it says nothing because no instance of true propositions can be enumerated with the guidance of the schema.
Horwich, in fact, I think he would respond like, saying that you cannot define truth, but it still has a meaning. Like you say, snow is white is true. For sure, it is true because snow is white. Once you have accepted that snow is white, you have to accept that it is true. We can check the following examples he gave.
Since I didn’t think Horwich explained it clearly in class, I would show some of my interpretations of his theory later.

SECTION 3 objections
Sten Lindström suggested my approach cannot explain how we might arrive at truth-claims such as:
(a) The Continuum Hypothesis is true.
(b) There are true propositions that aren’t supported by available evidence.
(c) Every sentence is such that either it or its negation is true.
(d) Most statements that Clinton made in his deposition were true.
And I must concede that minimalism lacks the resources to rearticulate any of those truth-claims without using the word “true.”
But Künne’s definition, by contrast, can rearticulate (a) and (b) but not (c) and (d).
But the minimalist has other resources: though we can’t define these claims without “true,” we can explain how we arrive at them.

For example, to reach (a):
We identify the Continuum Hypothesis, and we accept:
“ is the Continuum Hypothesis ↔ p”.
Thus by Leibniz’s Law we infer:
“The Continuum Hypothesis is true.”
==Comments==:  One may hold that he actually says nothing. The explanation was based on an extremely important premise, that is, one shall accept the continuum hypothesis.
We have to acknowledge that Horwich’s intention was to give nothing epistemic, no commitment to maths, no commitment to science, no commitment metaphysically to the world. However, he would claim that you shall accept the equivalence schema, and truth is governed by instances of the schema.
meaning of truth
relation_to_putnam

Similarly for (b):
Consider a proposition A which is neither supported nor unsupported by any evidence.
Thus at least one propositions are true and unsupported by evidence, that is:
A\,\vee\sim A
==Comments==: sophistry

For (c):
Start by accepting many instances:
Either A or \sim A,
Either B or \sim B, etc.
Generalize to:
“Every declarative (= proposition-expressing) sentence is such that either it, or its negation, is true.”
==Comments==: this is more like a correspondence theory. What I was thinking was taking the language where there is an excluded middle rule, which can be related to Putnam and Carnap as well.

For (d):
Find statements ,A_1,\,A_2.\,\dots , that Clinton made.
Determine which are true, then count how many.
SECTION 4 different languages
The issue here is how the two approaches under present consideration — mine and Künne’s — deal with the prospect of true statements articulated using sentences that aren’t translatable into our language.
For simplicity, let’s imagine that we understand nothing but English.
Suppose F is a language, many of whose sentences are not translatable into English.
But suppose F contains an operator, “\{Y\}”, that, when applied to any categorical sentence of F — e.g. FS(k) — yields a singular term, “\{Y\}(FS(k))”, which, like an English that-clause, refers to the proposition expressed by FS(k).
In that case, it could be that language F contains a word — perhaps “fooo” — whose meaning is the same as the English “true”.
For it could be that F-speakers are disposed to accept, for every p, instances of:
\{FS(n)\}\text{ is fooo} \Leftrightarrow FS(n)
And, if so, then the way that F-speakers use their word fooo is the same as the way in which English speakers use “true” — which is our disposition to accept instances of “the proposition that p is true \Leftrightarrow p”.
Presumably, some of F’s untranslatable-into-English sentences might be true.
But English speakers will not be able to tell whether or not this is so.
For only if we could translate FS(k) could we formulate the instance of our equivalence schema that would enable us to specify the truth-condition of FS(k).
And Künne’s definition of “x is true” couldn’t solve this problem either; for it will be impossible for us to tell whether or not:
(\exists p)\bigg( \{FS(k) \} = \ulcorner p\urcorner \wedge p  \bigg)
Comments: Frankly, I acknowledge Horwich’s argument that it is impossible for us to tell whether or not FS(k) is true. The answer is trivial because it is not English (or any other language that we perceive). In Künne’s schema, if we take the "=" just as the identity, then p is in F and if there is a way for us to know whether p holds, we can say that FS(k) is fooo in F, and true (in English) according to the biconditional. I think the result quite conforms to our intuition.
However, in Horwich’s schema, we have to take a step back and only commit to \{FS(n)\}\text{ is fooo} \Leftrightarrow FS(n).
In this sense, Künne’s truth holds across different languages, that is, he can assert the truth inside a language L with another language L', while Horwich can only assert the truth inside the language L by L. If I am right, then Künne’s truth has a more general meaning (if we regard it as merely a meaning, not definition) than Horwich’s. (haven't been discussed)
SECTION 5 Liar paradox
(Horwich’s writing was really messy, and I am rewriting in a relatively more formal way.)
Consider proposition p :
p\Leftrightarrow \ulcorner p \urcorner\text{ is false}
Of course, one could refute that such a self-inference could be illegitimate, but we have to acknowledge that in ordinary languages (English), such self-inferences are inevitable (because the language is too strong). Not to mention, in formal systems, you can even devise a self-inference by diag (PA).
Then consider the equivalence schema, we will get \ulcorner p\urcorner \text{ is true} \Leftrightarrow p, which is
\ulcorner p\urcorner \text{ is true} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad  \ulcorner p \urcorner\text{ is false}
Now we infer that p is both true and not true.
Horwich thinks that at least one of our assumptions must be given up. It could be “every contradiction is false”, or the above p doesn’t express a proposition.
Or alternatively, the assumption that every instance of the schema must be accepted.

It seems to me that this last alternative is the best way of escaping from the paradox. — For remember that minimalism’s meaning-theory demands no more than an inclination to accept instances of the equivalence schema. And in this case, the inclination is overwhelmed by the paradoxical consequences of accepting it.

Comments: I don’t like Horwich’s picture for two reasons. (Notice here I don’t mean he is not coherent, I just think it is not that minimalistic as he or I expected).
First, the disposal of the liar paradox indicates the redundancy in his theory. He didn’t explicitly introduce meta-language to defuse the liar paradox, but implicitly used an operational meta-language. He suggests that we should exclude some instances of the equivalence schema, where the operation “exclude” can only happen in a meta-language outside the object language where we were asserting truth. Then the problem arises if we contemplate the object language, for Horwich never said what the object language is. Is it PA? Is it SA? Or is it just ordinary language? If we add different language frameworks into the consideration (it is very natural if you are a minimalist like Horwich, because you want the truth to be perceived as easy as possible, so you can adjust your meta-language according to your object language), we might collapse into truth pluralism. Therefore, truth loses its status as a unified, stable, meaningful (this word is controversial though) concept.
Second, even though we fix the object language, merely denying that every instance conforms to the schema seems to cause more issues, for there are no clear instructions on which instance we shall give up the schema. One may say, the paradoxical propositions are countable since the words are finite in English (here and the discussion below can be related to an analogue of PA computability). However, Kripke has demonstrated that there is no algorithm to enumerate the paradoxical propositions recursively; that is, whether or not a sentence is paradoxical is not decidable. Then I would say the equivalence schema, as well as the operational meta-language, is flawed and leaky, since we don’t even know when the schema can not be applied.
SECTION 6 answer to 5 questions
Here are my answers to the 5 questions posed in the announcement of Vienna’s September 2024 conference on TRUTH.

Is truth definable?
The word “truth” is the name of the monadic property that’s attributed to a proposition when we predicate “true” of it. And properties aren’t objects of definition.
So I suspect the intended question is:
“Is the English word ‘true’ definable?”
What’s implied by an affirmative answer is that a good definition can be devised, where the potential disqualifying defects include:

reliance on a term (in the proposed defining expression) that’s no less in need of definition than “true” is, or
The proposed defining expression includes a term (e.g. “fact”) that’s pretty clearly defined in terms of “true.”

I think the best candidate for a good definition of “true” is Wolfgang Künne’s.
But one might well feel that its quality depends on whether a clarifying definition of “proposition” can be provided.
However, I must concede that the absence of any such clarification of “proposition” would count against my minimalist proposal no less than it counts against Wolfgang’s definition of “true”.
Remarks: Russel denied the existence of the proposition, but I am not sure whether it was in Horwich’s sense.
Horwich said to me multiple times that he doesn’t want an (analytic) definition for truth, and he thinks pursuing definitions leads to infinite regress. Therefore, he thinks we shall choose truth as the concept that has a meaning without definition to end the regress. (And meaning is just use, in a Wittgenstein’s sense)
What is most important here is that we have to understand that in this picture, there is no metaphysical commitment to truth; that is, the schema itself won’t give any more knowledge (or knowledge of knowledge) about the cognitive object. What else he would say may probably (given by GPT):

Truth is a logical tool, not a property of reality;
The equivalence schema is meaning-constitutive
You learn the meaning of “true” by learning a rule:
	Anytime you accept 𝑝, you are also inclined to accept “𝑝 is true”.


Is propositional quantification coherent?
Obviously, we can coherently quantify over propositions — e.g.:
“There is a proposition expressed by the English sentence, ‘Snow is white’ ”
Or in other words:
“(\existsx)(x is a proposition \wedge x is expressed in English by ‘Snow is white’).”
So I assume that the intended question is:
“Is it coherent to quantify into declarative-sentence positions?”
And to this very different question, my answer is also “YES.”
For, as I suggested in Section 2, it’s plausible that our acceptance of:
(\exists p)(\#...p)
consists in our acceptance of the instance of (\#...p).

phil_public/undefinability_of_i.title: undefinability_of_i
phil_public/undefinability_of_i.content:
metaphysics explanation maudlin kripke
This question was raised in Tim Maudlin’s lecture discussing naming and necessity. Tim was arguing that referring to something (especially pointing to something), say pointing to a book and claiming that it is blablabla, is purely an anaphoric chain and nothing causal was involved. Then one gave an instance that the imaginary unit i is not definable, but you can point to it on the complex plane (I guess that was what he was trying to say), which was refuted by Tim.

Undefinability in Model Theory
In model theory, a structure M (like \mathbb C) interprates a formal language L (like the language of fields).
A subset S\subseteq M^n is called definable if there is a formula \varphi(x_1,\dots,x_n) in L such that:
S = \{ (a_1,\dots,a_n) \in M^n : M \models \varphi(a_1,\dots,a_n)\}.
An element a\in M is definable if there is a formula \varphi(x) with exactly one solution in M, i.e has unique item preserving the formula true.
For our case, we need a first-order formula \varphi(x) such that:
\mathbb{C} \models \varphi(i) \quad \text{and} \quad \text{for all } a \in \mathbb{C}, \mathbb{C} \models \varphi(a) \rightarrow a = i.
This can be proved by an automorphism, and below is an informal proof.


                  
                  Definition of automorphism (informal) 
                  
                

A homomorphism between two L-structures M and N is a map h : |M| \to |N| that respects the structure:
h(f^M(a_1,\dots,a_n)) = f^N(h(a_1),\dots,h(a_n))
and for every relation symbol R,
(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in R^M \implies (h(a_1),\dots,h(a_n))\in R^N,
and constants are preserved: h(c^M)=c^N.
If the map h is bijective and its inverse is also a homomorphism, it’s an isomorphism.
If it’s an isomorphism from a structure onto itself, it’s an automorphism.
An important corollary is that, an automorphism preserves all the truths. For instance, for the field \mathbb C, any automorphism, say \sigma, preserves the field operation:
\sigma(z+w) = \sigma(z) + \sigma(w), \qquad \sigma(z \cdot w) = \sigma(z) \cdot \sigma(w),
and of course
\sigma(0)=0, \quad \sigma(1)=1.


                  
                  Fact 
                  
                

If a is definable (without parameters), then every automorphism of M fixes a


This fact is obvious from the above corollary, which suggests that
M \models \varphi(a) \implies M \models \varphi(f(a)),
and by uniqueness f(a) = a.


                  
                  Proposition 
                  
                

The imaginary unit i is not definable in \mathbb C.




                  
                  Proof 
                  
                

Consider the automorphism \sigma(a+bi) = a-bi, i.e. conjugation. The automorphism fixes only the real numbers. If i were definable in the language of field, then \sigma(i) = i, but according to the definition \sigma(i) = -i \neq i, contradicted.
So i is not definable.\qquad\square
